ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the isosceles $\triangle ABC$ is inscribed in $\odot O$, with $AB=AC$, and $\angle BAC=120^\circ$. Point $D$ is on the arc $AC$, and line $BD$ is drawn. Point $E$ is on line $BD$, satisfying $\angle ABE=\angle ECB$. If $CD=2$, what is the area of $\triangle AEC$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} As shown in the figure, connect $AD$,\\
since $AB=AC$ and $\angle BAC=120^\circ$,\\
thus $\angle ABC=\angle ACB=\frac{1}{2}\left(180^\circ-\angle BAC\right)=30^\circ$,\\
therefore $\angle ADB=\angle ACB=30^\circ$,\\
since $\angle ABE=\angle ECB$,\\
thus $\angle DEC=\angle DBC+\angle ECB=\angle DBC+\angle ABE=\angle ABC=30^\circ$,\\
therefore $\angle ADB=\angle DEC=30^\circ$,\\
hence $AD\parallel EC$,\\
thus the distance between $AD$ and $EC$ is equal everywhere,\\
therefore $\text{Area of }\triangle AEC=\text{Area of }\triangle DEC$,\\
since point D is a point on the arc $\overset{\frown}{AC}$,\\
thus $\angle EDC=\angle BAC=120^\circ$,\\
construct $DH\perp EC$ at point H,\\
since $\angle ABD=\angle ECB$ and $\angle ACD=\angle ABD$,\\
thus $\angle ACD=\angle ECB$,\\
since $\angle ACB=30^\circ$,\\
thus $\angle ACE+\angle ECB=30^\circ$,\\
thus $\angle ACE+\angle ACD=30^\circ$,\\
that is, $\angle DCE=30^\circ=\angle DEC$,\\
thus $\triangle DEC$ is an isosceles triangle,\\
since $CD=2$,\\
thus $DH=\frac{1}{2}CD=1$,\\
thus $CH=\sqrt{CD^{2}-DH^{2}}=\sqrt{3}$,\\
thus $EC=2\sqrt{3}$,\\
thus $\text{Area of }\triangle DEC=\frac{1}{2}EC\cdot DH=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\sqrt{3}\times 1=\boxed{\sqrt{3}}$.

Hence $\angle ADB=\angle DEC=30^\circ$, so $AD\parallel EC$. Therefore $\text{Area}(\triangle AEC)=\text{Area}(\triangle DEC)$. Since $D$ is on arc $AC$, $\angle EDC=\angle BAC=120^\circ$. Triangles AEC and DEC have EC as the same base, and A and D are on the line AD parallel to EC, so the heights of the two triangles are equal and their areas are equal, namely [AEC]=[DEC]. Now look at triangle DEC. Because E, B, D are collinear, ∠EDC=∠BDC. By the inscribed angle theorem, ∠BDC=∠BAC=120°, so ∠EDC=120°. In addition, ∠ABD=∠ACD; and E is on BD, so ∠ABE=∠ABD. raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, the isosceles $\triangle ABC$ is inscribed in $\odot O$, with $AB=AC$, and $\angle BAC=120^\circ$. Point $D$ is on arc $AC$, and line $BD$ is drawn. Point $E$ is on line $BD$, satisfying $\angle ABE=\angle ECB$. If $CD=2$, what is the area of $\triangle AEC$?
raw_record.answer: \textbf{Solution:} Connect $AD$. Since $AB=AC$ and $\angle BAC=120^\circ$, we have $\angle ABC=\angle ACB=\frac{1}{2}(180^\circ-120^\circ)=30^\circ$. Therefore $\angle ADB=\angle ACB=30^\circ$. Since $\angle ABE=\angle ECB$, then $\angle DEC=\angle DBC+\angle ECB=\angle DBC+\angle ABE=\angle ABC=30^\circ$. Hence $\angle ADB=\angle DEC=30^\circ$, so $AD\parallel EC$. Therefore $\text{Area}(\triangle AEC)=\text{Area}(\triangle DEC)$. Since $D$ is on arc $AC$, $\angle EDC=\angle BAC=120^\circ$. Construct $DH\perp EC$ at $H$. Since $\angle ABD=\angle ECB$ and $\angle ACD=\angle ABD$, we get $\angle ACD=\angle ECB$. Also, $\angle ACB=30^\circ$, so $\angle ACE+\angle ECB=30^\circ$, hence $\angle ACE+\angle ACD=30^\circ$, that is, $\angle DCE=30^\circ=\angle DEC$. Thus $\triangle DEC$ is isosceles. Since $CD=2$, $DH=\frac{1}{2}CD=1$, and $CH=\sqrt{CD^2-DH^2}=\sqrt{3}$. Thus $EC=2\sqrt{3}$, so $\text{Area}(\triangle DEC)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot EC\cdot DH=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\sqrt{3}\times 1=\boxed{\sqrt{3}}$.

A is above the circle, B is on the left side, C is on the right side, triangle ABC is inscribed in the circle, and AB and AC are two oblique sides, while BC is approximately horizontal. D is located on the upper minor arc from A to C, segment BD passes through the interior point E, EC is also drawn in the figure, and AD can be connected as an auxiliary line.

Reasoning: Because AB=AC and ∠BAC=120°, the base angles ∠ABC=∠ACB=(180°-120°)/2=30°. Connect AD. By the inscribed angle theorem, ∠ADB=∠ACB=30°. Also because E is on BD, and it is given that ∠ABE=∠ECB, ∠DEC=∠DBC+∠ECB=∠DBC+∠ABE=∠ABC=30°. Thus ∠ADB=∠DEC=30°, therefore AD ∥ EC. Triangles AEC and DEC have EC as the same base, and A and D are on the line AD parallel to EC, so the heights of the two triangles are equal and their areas are equal, namely [AEC]=[DEC].

Now look at triangle DEC. Because E, B, D are collinear, ∠EDC=∠BDC. By the inscribed angle theorem, ∠BDC=∠BAC=120°, so ∠EDC=120°. In addition, ∠ABD=∠ACD; and E is on BD, so ∠ABE=∠ABD. Combining ∠ABE=∠ECB, we get ∠ACD=∠ECB. Because ∠ACB=30°, ∠ACE+∠ECB=30°, hence ∠ACE+∠ACD=30°, that is, ∠DCE=30°. Therefore the three angles of △DEC are 30°, 120°, 30°, so DE=CD. It is known that CD=2, so DE=2. Thus [DEC]=(1/2)·CD·DE·sin120°=(1/2)·2·2·(√3/2)=√3. Since [AEC]=[DEC], the area of △AEC is √3.
